claims.text: FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles contain nanoscale local compositional fluctuations.
Some compositionally fluctuating regions have lower cohesive energy than the surrounding alloy.
Premelting initiated by local compositional fluctuations governs the overall melting behavior of FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles.
The initial particles are solid, homogeneous, single-phase, and nominally equiatomic in Fe, Ni, Cr, Co, and Cu.
Localized enrichment of lower-melting-point elements, or depletion of higher-melting-point elements, forms heterogeneous surface patches.
Compositionally heterogeneous surface patches lower the local energy barrier for melting.
The chemical complexity of high-entropy alloys intrinsically produces nanoscale compositional fluctuations.
Regions with subtly altered composition begin melting at lower temperatures because they have lower cohesive energy.
Initial microscopic melt pockets coalesce and propagate melting across the nanoparticle.
Premelting will first appear as discrete, compositionally distinct regions at particle surfaces.
Localized surface premelting will begin below the bulk melting point.
FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles will exhibit a broader melting curve than more chemically uniform baseline nanoparticles.
Comparable single-metal or binary nanoparticles melt uniformly without early localized premelting.
The proposed mechanism is limited to nanoscale, single-phase HEA particles under controlled, slow heating.
The mechanism may not apply to bulk materials or rapid heating because kinetic effects can obscure equilibrium compositional variations.
Prior mechanical-property studies support an influential role for chemical heterogeneity in HEA phase behavior.
Direct evidence connecting nanoscale compositional fluctuations to premelting in HEA nanoparticles is sparse.
Uniform melting without localized premelting, or behavior statistically indistinguishable from homogeneous controls, would falsify the proposed mechanism.
